newsitem.title: USA: Developing countries try gentler approach to G7.
newsitem.headline: Developing countries try gentler approach to G7.

text.p: The G24 group of developing countries decided on Saturday to drop its traditionally confrontational attitude towards the Group of Seven leading industrialized nations.

Finance officials of the G24, which groups African, Asian and Latin American countries, said after meeting at the annual gathering of the International Monetary Fund and World Bank, that they now wanted to try a more constructive approach to influence world financial policies.
"We want to give up the attitude of being vis-a-vis anyone," said the head of the G24, Qazi Alimullah, deputy chairman of the Planning Commission of Pakistan.
"We want to say that this is one global village," he added, noting that the end of the Cold War had set new conditions for international relations.

"We want to have a meaningful dialogue, we want to forge an alliance with them, so that at the international level, whatever decisions are taken, they are taken for the world as a whole, and not only for the OECD countries," he said.
The G24 was formed in 1977 at a meeting in Lima of the Group of 77 non-aligned nations to represent developing countries in international monetary negotiations.

The group includes Algeria, Argentina, Brazil, Colombia, Egypt, Ethiopia, Gabon, Ghana, Guatemala, India, Iran, Ivory Coast, Lebanon, Mexico, Nigeria, Pakistan, Peru, Philippines, Sri Lanka, Syria, Trinidad and Tobago, Venezuela and Zaire.

Venezuelan central bank president Antonio Casas, who is slated to take over as chairman in April, said that the G24 will seek to have a greater say in the discussion and shaping of international policy.
"We want to be proactive, not just reactive. We have to say what are the issues that interest us, and not just react to what the G7 or any other group of industrialized nations says," Casas said.
The G24 have long, if grudgingly, recognized that the affluent G7 countries call the shots at the IMF and the World Bank because they are the major shareholders at the Bretton Woods institutions.
Furthermore, the industrialized nations' policies greatly influence the economies of the rest of the world.

In a communique released by the G24 delegates after their deliberations at the annual meetings of the IMF and the World Bank, the developing countries had a few suggestions for their richer neighbors.
"Long-term interest rates remain high in real terms in international capital markets, pointing to the need for further progress in fiscal consolidation in major industrial countries," it said.
The G24 also urged the European nations to work on their unemployment by addressing labor market rigidities, pointing out that such problems often generate calls for protectionism.

"These protectionist pressures were particularly egregious when disguised under calls for environmental security, human rights, or higher labor standards in developing countries," added the statement.
As expected, the G24 backed a proposal for a special issue of the IMF's own currency, special drawing rights, that boost the ability of IMF members to borrow.

The G24 also supported the sale of some of the IMF's gold reserves to prop up the Fund's Enhanced Structural Adjustment Facility, an IMF loan program earmarked for both transition and highly indebted poor countries.
